prompt: An unresponsive adult has gurgling respirations and vomitus in the mouth. Your first airway action is to:

options.text: Log-roll, suction the oropharynx, then reassess breathing
Insert an oropharyngeal airway, then suction around it
Give two rescue breaths by pocket mask, then suction
Keep the patient supine and perform a head-tilt chin-lift

explanation: Airway obstruction from secretions requires positioning and suction before adjuncts or ventilation.

distractorExplanations.b: An OPA placed over vomitus can push material deeper; clear the airway with suction before inserting any adjunct.
distractorExplanations.c: Ventilating before clearing vomitus forces it into the lungs; suction first, then ventilate only if breathing is inadequate.
distractorExplanations.d: Supine positioning lets vomitus pool in the airway; the patient is rolled to the side so fluids drain and suction can clear them.

prompt: Which patient is the best candidate for a nasopharyngeal (NPA) airway?

options.text: Apneic patient requiring bag-mask ventilation
Semiconscious patient with intact gag reflex who needs basic airway support
Patient with suspected basilar skull fracture
Fully conscious patient refusing all care

explanation: NPA is tolerated in semiconscious patients with gag reflex; OPA may trigger gagging/vomiting.

distractorExplanations.a: BVM may be used without NPA; NPA helps maintain patency in some semiconscious patients.
distractorExplanations.c: NPA is contraindicated with basilar skull fracture risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Refusal limits intervention.

prompt: Proper head-tilt chin-lift is contraindicated when you suspect

options.text: Asthma exacerbation
Loose dentures in the mouth
Cervical spine injury
An unresponsive patient with a gag reflex

explanation: Suspected spinal injury requires jaw-thrust/manual inline stabilization instead of head-tilt.

distractorExplanations.a: Airway opening may still be needed with spinal precautions.
distractorExplanations.b: Loose dentures are removed before ventilation, but they do not make the head-tilt chin-lift contraindicated.
distractorExplanations.d: A present gag reflex contraindicates an oropharyngeal airway, not the manual head-tilt chin-lift maneuver.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: A conscious adult is choking, cannot speak, and has ineffective cough. You should

options.text: Encourage forceful coughing and monitor closely
Give 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts as for an infant
Perform a blind finger sweep to remove the object
Give abdominal thrusts until obstruction clears

explanation: Complete airway obstruction in a conscious adult warrants abdominal thrusts per AHA BLS. Continue until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unresponsive, then begin CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: Coughing is encouraged only when the cough is effective; a silent, ineffective cough means severe obstruction needing thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: Back blows alternating with chest thrusts is the infant sequence; a conscious choking adult receives abdominal thrusts.
distractorExplanations.c: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only an object you can see, and use abdominal thrusts first.

prompt: When ventilating an apneic adult with a bag-valve-mask (BVM), adequate ventilation is indicated by?

options.text: Visible chest rise over about 1 second per breath
Abdominal rise with each squeeze of the bag
Breaths delivered at 30 per minute to raise SpO2 quickly
An SpO2 rise within the first 10 seconds of bagging

explanation: Each breath should produce visible chest rise without excessive rate or force. Deliver about 10–12 breaths per minute for an apneic adult with a pulse.

distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal rise means air is entering the stomach from excess volume or poor head position, not effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty breaths per minute is hyperventilation; it causes gastric inflation and reduces venous return and cardiac output.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse oximetry lags behind changes in ventilation; visible chest rise is the immediate bedside indicator.

prompt: An oropharyngeal airway (OPA) is sized by measuring from:

options.text: Tip of the nose to the earlobe on the same side
Corner of the mouth to the angle of the mandible
Bridge of the nose to the cleft of the chin
Width of the patient's little finger

explanation: Standard OPA sizing uses mouth corner to mandibular angle.

distractorExplanations.a: Nose-tip-to-earlobe is the sizing method for a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA), not an oropharyngeal airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Bridge of nose to chin cleft is how a BVM or pocket mask is sized, not the length of an OPA.
distractorExplanations.d: Little-finger width is a rough guide to airway tube diameter, not the length measurement used for an OPA.

prompt: You are ventilating a patient with a BVM and resistance is high with poor chest rise. You should first

options.text: Squeeze the bag harder to overcome the resistance
Switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Reposition the head/jaw and confirm a mask seal
Begin abdominal thrusts for a foreign-body airway

explanation: Poor rise often reflects inadequate seal or airway positioning before increasing force/rate.

distractorExplanations.a: More force increases gastric inflation without fixing the cause; poor chest rise usually means poor position or seal.
distractorExplanations.b: A nonrebreather does not ventilate; a patient who needs BVM support still needs positive-pressure breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: Thrusts are for obstruction that persists after the airway is repositioned; reposition and check the seal first.

prompt: Which finding suggests partial upper airway obstruction?

options.text: Silent chest with no air movement
Expiratory wheezing heard in both lungs
Crackles at both lung bases on inhalation
Stridor with hoarse voice and anxiety

explanation: Stridor and voice changes suggest partial obstruction of the upper airway.

distractorExplanations.a: Complete obstruction may be silent.
distractorExplanations.b: Diffuse expiratory wheezing reflects lower airway bronchoconstriction, not partial upper airway obstruction.
distractorExplanations.c: Crackles indicate fluid in the alveoli, such as pulmonary edema, which is a lower airway finding.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: For a trauma patient requiring spinal precautions, opening the airway is best done with:

options.text: Jaw-thrust while maintaining manual inline stabilization
Head-tilt chin-lift with a cervical collar applied
Modified chin-lift with the head turned to one side
Nasopharyngeal airway insertion before any manual maneuver

explanation: Jaw-thrust minimizes cervical motion when spinal injury is suspected.

distractorExplanations.b: Head-tilt chin-lift extends the neck even with a collar in place; jaw-thrust with manual stabilization is used instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Turning the head rotates the cervical spine; the head is held neutral and inline while the jaw is thrust forward.
distractorExplanations.d: An adjunct comes after the airway is opened manually, and NPAs are avoided with suspected facial or basilar skull fractures.

prompt: A patient with COPD receiving emergency oxygen via nonrebreather at 15 L/min becomes sleepy with shallow respirations. The EMR should

options.text: Continue 15 L/min by nonrebreather and recheck in 15 minutes
Reassess ventilatory effort and follow local protocol
Turn off the oxygen to restore the hypoxic drive
Insert an OPA to keep the sleepy patient's airway open

explanation: COPD patients may depend on hypoxic drive; titrate per protocol and monitor ventilatory status. Local COPD protocols typically call for titrated oxygen, with assisted ventilation if breathing becomes inadequate.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving high-flow oxygen unchanged for 15 minutes ignores a falling ventilatory effort; reassess now and assist as needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypoxia kills faster than CO2 retention; oxygen is titrated per protocol, not withdrawn from a hypoxic patient.
distractorExplanations.d: An OPA is for unresponsive patients without a gag reflex; a sleepy patient who still gags will vomit or retch.

prompt: Suctioning the oropharynx should generally be limited to:

options.text: 5 seconds, with no reoxygenation between passes
Continuous passes until the airway is fully clear
10 seconds with reoxygenation between attempts
30 seconds per pass to clear thick secretions

explanation: Brief suction passes reduce hypoxia risk; reoxygenate between attempts.

distractorExplanations.a: Five seconds is the infant guideline, and every pass removes oxygen, so reoxygenation between attempts is still needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuous suction causes hypoxia and vagal bradycardia; suction in brief passes with reoxygenation in between.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty-second passes cause hypoxia; for thick secretions, use brief passes and alternate with ventilation.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Which oxygen delivery device provides the highest FiO2 when fitted properly?

options.text: Nasal cannula at 6 L/min, its maximum flow
Simple face mask at 10 L/min without a reservoir bag
Venturi mask set to a 40% oxygen concentration
Nonrebreather mask with reservoir at adequate flow

explanation: A nonrebreather with reservoir and sufficient flow can deliver high FiO2.

distractorExplanations.a: A nasal cannula at 6 L/min delivers only about 44% oxygen, far below a nonrebreather with reservoir.
distractorExplanations.b: A simple mask tops out around 40–60%; without a reservoir bag it cannot match a nonrebreather's concentration.
distractorExplanations.c: A Venturi delivers precise low-to-moderate fixed concentrations (about 24–50%), below a nonrebreather.

prompt: An apneic adult patient after successful ROSC from CPR should receive

options.text: Oxygen and ventilatory support per protocol
Nonrebreather oxygen at 15 L/min without ventilations
Chest compressions resumed at 100–120 per minute
Rapid ventilation at 30 breaths/min to clear CO2

explanation: Post-ROSC patients often need oxygen and ventilatory support with close monitoring. Monitor with pulse oximetry and reassess often.

distractorExplanations.b: An apneic patient cannot draw in nonrebreather oxygen; apnea after ROSC still requires positive-pressure ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: ROSC means a pulse is present; compressions resume only if the pulse is lost again.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilation after ROSC lowers cardiac output and cerebral blood flow; ventilate about 10 times per minute.

prompt: When using a pocket mask with a one-way valve, the EMR should?

options.text: Deliver large, forceful breaths to overcome the valve
Deliver breaths over 1 second watching for chest rise
Remove the one-way valve to deliver more air volume
Seal the mask over the mouth only, leaving the nose open

explanation: Pocket mask ventilations follow BLS guidelines: slow breaths with visible rise.

distractorExplanations.a: The one-way valve adds little resistance; forceful breaths inflate the stomach and raise the risk of vomiting.
distractorExplanations.c: The valve protects the rescuer from exhaled air and fluids; removing it adds infection risk without improving ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: The pocket mask covers both mouth and nose; leaving the nose open lets air escape and causes poor chest rise.

prompt: Signs of worsening upper airway swelling (e.g., anaphylaxis) include

options.text: Expiratory wheezing with a prolonged exhalation phase
Hives spreading across the chest, back, and arms
Progressive stridor, drooling, and difficulty swallowing
Crackles at both lung bases with pink, frothy sputum production

explanation: Stridor, drooling, and dysphagia suggest impending complete airway obstruction.

distractorExplanations.a: Wheezing reflects lower airway bronchospasm; upper airway swelling shows inspiratory stridor and voice change.
distractorExplanations.b: Spreading hives show skin involvement of the allergic reaction, not narrowing of the upper airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Crackles and frothy sputum suggest pulmonary edema in the alveoli, not swelling of the upper airway.

prompt: Direct pressure fails to control severe extremity bleeding. Your next step is

options.text: Add more gauze and press harder for 10 more minutes
Elevate the leg and compress the femoral pressure point
Apply a tourniquet directly over the wound site
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound

explanation: Life-threatening extremity hemorrhage uncontrolled by pressure warrants tourniquet application with time documented. Note the time the tourniquet was applied.

distractorExplanations.a: Once direct pressure has failed on severe extremity bleeding, more pressure time delays definitive control by tourniquet.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended for severe bleeding; they delay tourniquet application.
distractorExplanations.c: A tourniquet goes 2–3 inches proximal to the wound, not on it, so it compresses the artery above the bleed.

prompt: A helmeted motorcycle rider is awake with stable vitals after a crash. Helmet removal should occur when

options.text: Airway or breathing cannot be managed with helmet in place
Before applying a cervical collar on every helmeted rider
When the patient reports neck pain or tingling in the hands
When the face shield must be lifted to assess the patient

explanation: Helmets remain if airway is manageable; remove when airway/breathing needs require it with spinal precautions. Vomiting that cannot be cleared with the helmet on is another indication.

distractorExplanations.b: Routine removal is not required; a snug helmet that allows airway access stays on with manual stabilization.
distractorExplanations.c: Neck pain or tingling suggests spinal injury, a reason to minimize movement, not to remove a helmet that allows airway care.
distractorExplanations.d: The shield or face mask can be lifted or removed without taking off the helmet; removal is reserved for airway problems.

prompt: Which patient should be immobilized on a long backboard per typical EMR protocols?

options.text: Stable alert patient who walked away without complaint
Mechanism suggesting spinal injury with midline tenderness or neurologic deficit
Any patient with a sprained finger
Patient refusing all care but fully neurologically intact without tenderness

explanation: Spinal motion restriction is indicated with concerning mechanism plus exam findings.

distractorExplanations.a: Low suspicion with normal exam may not require immobilization per local protocol.
distractorExplanations.c: Finger sprain alone does not indicate spinal injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Competent refusal may limit immobilization.

prompt: Signs of shock from hemorrhage include

options.text: Warm, flushed skin with a slow pulse and a low blood pressure
High blood pressure, a slow pulse, and irregular breathing
Pale cool clammy skin, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill
Hot, dry, flushed skin with a rapid pulse and confusion

explanation: Hypovolemic shock often presents with tachycardia, poor perfusion, and altered mental status.

distractorExplanations.a: Warm skin with bradycardia and hypotension describes neurogenic shock, not hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock.
distractorExplanations.b: That is Cushing's triad of rising intracranial pressure, not the picture of shock from hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.d: Hot, dry skin with confusion suggests heat stroke; hemorrhage causes pale, cool, clammy skin.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: An open fracture of the forearm with active bleeding should be managed by:

options.text: Realigning the exposed bone end into the wound, then splinting it
Applying a tourniquet first for any bleeding open fracture
Wrapping tightly with an elastic bandage before splinting the arm
Covering with sterile dressing, controlling bleeding, and splinting

explanation: Do not replace exposed bone; cover, control hemorrhage, immobilize, and transport. Splint the limb in the position found.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling exposed bone back into the wound contaminates deep tissue; cover it and splint without reducing it.
distractorExplanations.b: Most open-fracture bleeding stops with direct pressure; a tourniquet is reserved for life-threatening bleeding pressure cannot control.
distractorExplanations.c: A tight elastic wrap over an open fracture can cut off distal circulation; use a sterile dressing and check CMS before and after.

prompt: When splinting a painful swollen ankle, the EMR should:

options.text: Splint in the position of comfort after neurovascular check
Force the foot into anatomical neutral despite severe pain
Remove the shoe and leave the joint unsupported
Apply heat before assessment

explanation: Splinting in position found after CMS check reduces movement and pain.

distractorExplanations.b: Forcing alignment can worsen injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Immobilization is indicated for suspected fracture/sprain.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat is not initial care for acute trauma.

prompt: A patient impaled by a metal rod through the abdomen should receive

options.text: Immediate removal of the object to bandage the hole
Stabilization of the object in place and rapid transport
Cutting the rod flush with the skin to ease transport
Removal of the rod if bleeding soaks through the dressing

explanation: Impaled objects remain in place unless they block airway management per medical direction.

distractorExplanations.a: Removal can cause uncontrolled hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting transmits motion into the wound; an object is shortened only if needed, by rescuers, while it is stabilized.
distractorExplanations.d: Increased bleeding is controlled with pressure around the object; removal can release a tamponaded vessel and worsen hemorrhage.

prompt: Which burn should receive priority cooling and transport consideration?

options.text: Superficial sunburn covering most of the back and both shoulders
Small full-thickness burn on the forearm with charred, painless, leathery skin
Partial-thickness burn to circumferential chest with singed nasal hairs
Partial-thickness burn to the front of one thigh, about 4% BSA

explanation: Circumferential chest burns and inhalation signs suggest airway/ventilation risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Superficial burns are not counted in critical burn size; airway involvement and circumferential burns take priority.
distractorExplanations.b: A small full-thickness burn away from critical areas is serious but lacks the airway threat of an inhalation injury.
distractorExplanations.d: About 4% partial-thickness on one thigh is a minor-to-moderate burn without airway or circumferential involvement.

prompt: Tension pneumothorax signs may include

options.text: Muffled heart tones, distended neck veins, and low BP
Bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular breathing
Paradoxical movement of a chest segment on breathing
Tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, and shock

explanation: Tension pneumothorax causes unilateral absent sounds, JVD, hypotension, and possible tracheal shift. Tracheal deviation is away from the affected side and is a late sign.

distractorExplanations.a: Muffled heart tones with JVD and hypotension are Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade; breath sounds stay equal.
distractorExplanations.b: That is Cushing's triad of rising intracranial pressure, not a sign of tension pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.c: Paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment is the sign of a flail chest, not tension pneumothorax.

prompt: During manual inline stabilization, the EMR holding the head should

options.text: Maintain alignment until immobilization is coordinated
Release once a properly sized cervical collar is in place
Return the head to neutral even if pain or resistance occurs
Apply gentle upward traction to stretch the cervical spine

explanation: Inline stabilization continues until an coordinated team applies collar/board. Release only when the collar and full spinal motion restriction are in place.

distractorExplanations.b: A collar alone does not fully restrict motion; manual stabilization continues until the patient is secured to the device.
distractorExplanations.c: Movement to neutral stops if it causes pain, resistance, or new deficits; the head is then held in the position found.
distractorExplanations.d: Traction on the neck can pull apart an unstable injury; the head is held inline without pulling.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: A patient with an amputated finger should have the part

options.text: Placed directly on ice in a cooler to slow tissue death
Wrapped moist in sterile gauze, placed in waterproof bag on ice
Submerged in a sealed container of sterile saline and kept cool
Wrapped in dry gauze and kept at room temperature in a bag

explanation: Amputated parts are kept cool and moist without direct ice contact for possible reattachment. Do not let the part touch the ice directly.

distractorExplanations.a: Direct ice contact freezes and damages tissue; the bagged part rests on ice or cold packs without touching ice.
distractorExplanations.c: Immersion waterlogs the tissue and hampers reattachment; the part is wrapped in moistened gauze, not soaked.
distractorExplanations.d: Warm tissue deteriorates faster; the bagged part must be kept cool to extend the window for reattachment.

prompt: The primary purpose of the primary trauma survey (ABCDE) is to:

options.text: Complete full patient history before any interventions
Obtain insurance information first
Identify and treat immediate life threats in sequence
Splint all injuries before airway assessment

explanation: ABCDE prioritizes life threats: airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure.

distractorExplanations.a: History follows stabilization.
distractorExplanations.b: Insurance is secondary.
distractorExplanations.d: Airway comes before detailed splinting.

prompt: A flail chest segment may cause

options.text: Tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds on one side
Muffled heart sounds with distended neck veins and low BP
Inspiratory stridor from swelling of the upper airway
Paradoxical chest wall movement and respiratory distress

explanation: Multiple rib fractures create unstable segment with paradoxical motion and hypoventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Tracheal shift with absent breath sounds is tension pneumothorax; flail chest shows a segment moving opposite the chest wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Muffled heart sounds, JVD, and hypotension point to cardiac tamponade, not a flail chest segment.
distractorExplanations.c: Stridor is an upper airway sign; a flail chest impairs chest wall mechanics and causes hypoventilation.

prompt: When assessing pulse, motor, and sensation (CMS) distal to an injury, absent distal pulse after splinting means?

options.text: Loosen/adjust splint and reassess; prepare for rapid transport
Tighten the splint to control swelling and recheck in 15 minutes
Document it as expected after splinting and continue transport
Elevate the limb above the heart to improve circulation

explanation: Loss of distal pulse after immobilization requires adjustment and urgent transport.

distractorExplanations.b: A tight splint can occlude circulation; loss of a distal pulse after splinting means loosening and adjusting it now.
distractorExplanations.c: A new pulse loss is not expected; it signals compromised circulation that needs adjustment and urgent reassessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Elevation does not restore arterial flow blocked by a tight splint; loosen and readjust, then recheck the pulse.

prompt: Scene size-up for trauma should include

options.text: BSI, the chief complaint, SAMPLE history, and baseline vitals
BSI, scene safety, mechanism, number of patients
Primary survey of airway, breathing, and circulation
Scene safety, then rapid trauma exam of the worst patient

explanation: Standard scene approach emphasizes safety, BSI, MOI, and resource requests. Size-up also identifies the need for additional resources.

distractorExplanations.a: Chief complaint, SAMPLE history, and vitals belong to patient assessment, which begins after the scene size-up.
distractorExplanations.c: The primary survey follows scene size-up; it is not part of evaluating hazards, mechanism, and resource needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Size-up must also count patients and request resources before committing to one patient's exam.

prompt: You find an unresponsive adult without pulse. After activating EMS and getting an AED, you should

options.text: Give 2 rescue breaths, then check the pulse again
Give rescue breaths at 1 every 6 seconds
Start chest compressions at 100–120/min
Start compressions at 60–80/min to limit rib injury

explanation: BLS for adult cardiac arrest emphasizes immediate high-quality compressions and early AED. Allow full chest recoil between compressions.

distractorExplanations.a: Adult CPR starts with compressions (C-A-B); repeating pulse checks delays compressions in a confirmed arrest.
distractorExplanations.b: Rescue breathing alone is for a patient who has a pulse; a pulseless patient needs chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: The guideline rate is 100–120 per minute; slower compressions reduce blood flow generated during CPR.

prompt: FAST stroke assessment includes checking for:

options.text: Facial droop, arm drift, speech, and current blood glucose level
Facial droop, abdominal pain, slurred speech, and temperature
Fixed pupils, abnormal posturing, seizures, and trauma
Facial droop, arm drift, speech difficulty, and time of onset

explanation: Face, Arms, Speech, Time helps identify stroke and urgency for transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Glucose is checked to rule out hypoglycemia mimics, but the T in FAST is time of onset (last known well).
distractorExplanations.b: The A in FAST is arm drift, not abdominal pain, and temperature is not a FAST element.
distractorExplanations.c: Pupils and posturing are head-injury and GCS findings, not the elements of FAST stroke screening.

prompt: A diabetic patient is confused, diaphoretic, and tremulous with a glucose of 52 mg/dL. You should

options.text: Administer oral glucose if awake and able to swallow safely
Assist with the patient's own insulin pen to correct the sugar
Wait to recheck glucose in 15 minutes before treating
Withhold oral glucose because the patient is confused

explanation: Conscious hypoglycemia with intact swallow gets fast-acting oral glucose per protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Insulin lowers glucose further; it treats hyperglycemia and would worsen this patient's hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.c: A symptomatic glucose of 52 mg/dL is treated now; the 15-minute recheck comes after giving oral glucose.
distractorExplanations.d: Confusion alone does not bar oral glucose if the patient is awake, follows commands, and swallows safely.

prompt: Anaphylaxis with wheeze and hypotension after bee sting requires:

options.text: Oral diphenhydramine and transport if the hives spread
Epinephrine auto-injector per protocol and rapid transport
High-flow oxygen and observation for 30 minutes on scene
Scraping the stinger, then rapid transport without medication

explanation: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM epinephrine and urgent ALS/transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Antihistamines do not reverse hypotension or bronchospasm; anaphylaxis needs epinephrine first.
distractorExplanations.c: Oxygen supports but does not reverse anaphylaxis; delaying epinephrine and transport worsens outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing the stinger is fine but secondary; wheeze and hypotension mean systemic anaphylaxis needing epinephrine.

prompt: A patient with crushing substernal chest pain and nitroglycerin prescribed should receive NTG only if

options.text: Systolic BP is adequate per protocol and patient has not taken PDE-5 inhibitor recently
Patient took sildenafil within 24–48 hours per drug interaction rules
Patient is hypotensive below 90 systolic
Pain is clearly from ankle sprain

explanation: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated in hypotension and recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.

distractorExplanations.a: Adequate BP and no recent PDE-5 use are required.
distractorExplanations.b: PDE-5 interaction risks severe hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Chest pain protocol applies to suspected cardiac pain.

prompt: Syncope with rapid recovery in a hot environment suggests

options.text: Heat stroke needing ice-water immersion
A seizure disorder; protect from injury
Simple fainting; no assessment is needed
Heat-related illness; move to cool area

explanation: Heat exhaustion/syncope needs cooling, rest, and assessment for worsening heat stroke. Assess hydration and perfusion after moving the patient.

distractorExplanations.a: Heat stroke presents with persistent altered mental status and hot skin; rapid recovery points to heat syncope or exhaustion.
distractorExplanations.b: A brief faint with quick recovery in the heat fits heat syncope; a seizure is typically followed by a postictal period.
distractorExplanations.c: Even with rapid recovery, syncope needs assessment for heat illness, dehydration, and cardiac causes.

prompt: Seizure activity has stopped and the patient is postictal but breathing adequately. You should

options.text: Place in recovery position, protect from injury, monitor airway
Restrain the limbs loosely to prevent a second seizure
Insert an oral airway to hold the airway open while drowsy
Keep the patient supine and recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes

explanation: Post-seizure care focuses on airway, protection, oxygen if needed, and evaluation. Time the event and arrange transport for evaluation.

distractorExplanations.b: Restraint does not prevent recurrent seizures and can cause injury; protect the patient from surrounding objects instead.
distractorExplanations.c: An OPA triggers gagging and vomiting in a postictal patient with a gag reflex; positioning and suction manage the airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Supine positioning lets secretions pool in the airway; the recovery position with continuous airway monitoring is needed.

prompt: Which vital sign pattern suggests decompensated shock in a medical patient?

options.text: Heart rate 118, BP 124/82, cool pale skin, anxious but alert
Heart rate 130, BP 86/60, cool skin, altered mental status
Heart rate 60, BP 168/98, slow irregular breathing, drowsy
Heart rate 104, BP 132/88, flushed warm skin, alert

explanation: Tachycardia, hypotension, poor perfusion, and AMS suggest shock.

distractorExplanations.a: Tachycardia and cool skin with a normal BP is compensated shock; decompensation adds falling BP and altered mentation.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypertension with a slow pulse and irregular breathing is Cushing's triad of rising ICP, not shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild tachycardia with a normal BP and warm skin lacks the hypotension and poor perfusion of decompensated shock.

prompt: A patient with asthma has silent chest and exhaustion. This indicates

options.text: Improving airflow after the inhaler has taken effect
An anxiety reaction causing shallow breathing
Impending respiratory failure requiring urgent transport
A mild attack that can be managed on scene with rest and oxygen

explanation: Silent chest and fatigue are ominous signs of severe bronchospasm/respiratory failure. Request advanced care early.

distractorExplanations.a: Less wheezing with exhaustion means too little air is moving to wheeze; a silent chest is ominous, not improvement.
distractorExplanations.b: Exhaustion with a silent chest is respiratory failure; attributing it to anxiety delays ventilation and transport.
distractorExplanations.d: A silent chest is a late, life-threatening sign; it calls for ventilatory support and rapid transport, not on-scene care.

prompt: For suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression, EMR care includes:

options.text: Sternal rubs and loud verbal stimulation to rouse the patient, then transport
Naloxone first, holding ventilations until it takes effect
High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask, then transport
Airway/ventilation support, naloxone per protocol, and transport

explanation: Opioid overdose management prioritizes ventilation and naloxone when authorized.

distractorExplanations.a: Stimulation does not correct respiratory depression; inadequate breathing needs BVM ventilation and naloxone per protocol.
distractorExplanations.b: Naloxone takes minutes and may be insufficient; ventilate with a BVM while naloxone is given.
distractorExplanations.c: A nonrebreather cannot help slow, shallow breathing; respiratory depression requires assisted BVM ventilation.

prompt: Chest pain patient with aspirin allergy and no contraindications otherwise: aspirin should be

options.text: Given if protocol allows after allergy assessment
Given at a reduced dose of 81 mg to lower the reaction risk
Replaced by oral diphenhydramine before giving aspirin
Withheld and patient left without transport

explanation: True aspirin allergy contraindicates; otherwise chewable aspirin may be given per protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: A lower dose does not prevent an allergic reaction; a true aspirin allergy is a contraindication to aspirin.
distractorExplanations.c: Premedicating with an antihistamine does not make aspirin safe in a true allergy and is outside EMR scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Transport still required.

prompt: A febrile patient with altered mental status and hot dry skin may have

options.text: Heat exhaustion needing rest and oral fluids
Heat stroke requiring rapid cooling and transport
Hypoglycemia needing oral glucose and observation
Heat cramps relieved by stretching and electrolytes

explanation: Heat stroke presents with CNS dysfunction and hot skin; it is life-threatening.

distractorExplanations.a: Heat exhaustion keeps mental status near normal with moist skin; altered mentation with hot, dry skin is heat stroke.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypoglycemia causes cool, clammy skin; fever with hot, dry skin and altered mentation points to heat stroke.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat cramps cause painful muscle spasms with normal mentation, not altered mental status and hot, dry skin.

prompt: When assisting a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, the injection site is typically?

options.text: Upper outer buttock (gluteal muscle)
Back of the upper arm (subcutaneous)
Outer mid-thigh (vastus lateralis)
Inner thigh near the femoral artery

explanation: Auto-injectors are administered IM in the anterolateral thigh.

distractorExplanations.a: Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh; gluteal injection risks fat deposition or sciatic nerve injury.
distractorExplanations.b: Subcutaneous absorption is slower; epinephrine auto-injectors deliver an IM dose into the lateral thigh.
distractorExplanations.d: The inner thigh lies over major vessels and nerves; the auto-injector goes into the outer (lateral) thigh.

prompt: Priority for a patient with severe abdominal pain and rigid abdomen includes:

options.text: Small sips of water and an antacid, then monitor vitals
Lay supine with legs straight and palpate the painful area first
Apply a heat pack to the abdomen and observe on scene
Keep NPO, monitor vitals, position of comfort, rapid transport

explanation: Acute rigid abdomen may indicate surgical emergency; NPO and urgent transport are key.

distractorExplanations.a: A rigid abdomen may need surgery; anything by mouth risks vomiting and aspiration, so the patient stays NPO.
distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal pain patients usually prefer knees flexed, and the painful quadrant is palpated last to avoid guarding.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat can mask worsening signs, and a rigid abdomen suggests a surgical emergency that needs rapid transport.

prompt: Pulse oximetry reading 88% on room air in a symptomatic patient should prompt

options.text: Oxygen per protocol and reassessment of work of breathing
Recheck the probe placement and wait for symptoms to worsen
Oxygen only if the reading falls below 85% on recheck
BVM ventilation even though breathing is adequate

explanation: Hypoxemia with symptoms warrants supplemental oxygen and further assessment/transport.

distractorExplanations.b: Checking probe placement is reasonable, but a symptomatic patient at 88% needs oxygen now, not delayed treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: Below about 94% in a symptomatic patient, oxygen is indicated; waiting for 85% delays needed treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: BVM ventilation is for inadequate breathing; adequate breathing with hypoxemia needs supplemental oxygen.

prompt: Upon arrival at a motor vehicle collision, the EMR's first priority is

options.text: Patient care before any scene safety assessment
Determine scene safety and use appropriate PPE
Interview witnesses for legal statements
Begin triage without notifying dispatch of hazards

explanation: Scene safety and BSI precede patient contact per standard EMS operations.

distractorExplanations.a: Unsafe scenes endanger responders and patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Witnesses are secondary to safety and care.
distractorExplanations.d: Communicate hazards and request resources.

prompt: A competent adult refuses transport after assessment. The EMR should

options.text: Transport anyway under implied consent for safety
Accept a verbal refusal and leave without documenting
Explain risks, ensure understanding, and document refusal
Ask police to place the patient in protective custody

explanation: Informed refusal requires capacity assessment, risk explanation, documentation, and medical control if needed. Leave contact and return instructions per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Implied consent applies only to patients who cannot decide; a competent adult has the right to refuse transport.
distractorExplanations.b: Refusals carry high liability; the risks explained, capacity, and the patient's signature must be documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Police custody is for patients who lack capacity or are a danger to themselves; a competent adult may refuse care.

prompt: Protected health information (PHI) on a PCR may be shared with:

options.text: Family members who call asking about the patient
Reporters at the scene if the patient's name is omitted
Fellow EMTs at other agencies for case review on social media
Receiving facility and personnel involved in patient care

explanation: HIPAA permits disclosure for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations on need-to-know basis.

distractorExplanations.a: Without the patient's permission, family callers are not authorized recipients; HIPAA allows sharing for treatment.
distractorExplanations.b: Other details can still identify a patient; media disclosure requires authorization, not just an omitted name.
distractorExplanations.c: Posting case details publicly breaches PHI even for education; sharing is limited to those involved in care.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: Standard precautions require

options.text: Gloves and hand hygiene at minimum
Gloves only when the patient appears to be bleeding
Hand sanitizer instead of gloves for fluid contact
N95 respirators and gowns on every call

explanation: Standard precautions treat all blood/body fluids as potentially infectious. Use them whenever contact with blood or body fluids is possible.

distractorExplanations.b: Standard precautions treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, not only visible bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand hygiene complements but does not replace gloves when contact with body fluids is expected.
distractorExplanations.d: N95s and gowns are transmission-based precautions for specific risks, not the standard-precautions minimum.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: When requesting additional resources, the EMR should provide?

options.text: Patient vital signs and chief complaints for each patient
Location, hazards, number of patients, and resources needed
The mechanism of injury and which driver appears to be at fault
A request made after all patients have been triaged

explanation: Clear concise radio/reporting includes location, problem, hazards, and resource needs. Also state the nature of the incident.

distractorExplanations.a: Detailed vitals belong in the hospital report; a resource request needs location, hazards, patient count, and resources.
distractorExplanations.c: Fault is irrelevant to a resource request; dispatch needs location, hazards, and the number of patients.
distractorExplanations.d: Additional resources are requested early during size-up; waiting until triage ends delays help.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: Medical direction may be required for:

options.text: Routine skills already covered by standing orders
Starting CPR on a pulseless adult who has no valid DNR order
Certain medications or protocols outside standing orders
Applying oxygen to a hypoxic patient by protocol

explanation: Online/offline medical control governs extensions beyond standing orders and some refusals. Complex refusals may also need medical direction per local policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Standing orders are offline medical direction; skills they cover need no online contact.
distractorExplanations.b: CPR on a pulseless patient is a standing-order BLS action; it does not wait for online medical direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen for hypoxia is covered by standing protocols; online direction is for actions beyond them.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: At a hazardous materials incident, the EMR should

options.text: Enter the warm zone to begin decontaminating the patients early
Approach from downwind to read the placard up close
Rinse contaminated patients before removing their clothing
Recognize hazard, protect self, and request hazmat specialists

explanation: Hazmat scenes require recognition, isolation, and specialist response beyond EMR scope. Deny entry to the area.

distractorExplanations.a: Decontamination in the warm zone requires hazmat training and PPE; awareness-level EMRs stay in the cold zone.
distractorExplanations.b: Approach is from upwind and uphill, and placards are read from a safe distance with binoculars.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing clothing removes most contamination first, and decontamination is done by trained hazmat teams.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Documentation on the PCR should be

options.text: Objective, timely, and include assessment findings
Written later from memory once the shift has ended
Corrected by erasing errors so the record looks clean
Focused on your opinion of the patient's behavior

explanation: Accurate objective documentation supports continuity of care and legal record. Also record interventions and the patient's responses.

distractorExplanations.b: Delayed documentation loses accuracy and timeliness; the PCR is completed as soon as possible after the call.
distractorExplanations.c: Errors are corrected with a single line, initials, and date; erasing or obliterating looks like falsification.
distractorExplanations.d: Subjective judgments about behavior invite liability; record objective findings and quote the patient.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: During mass casualty triage, a patient with absent respirations after airway opening may be classified

options.text: Immediate/red because airway opening was needed
Expectant/black in many triage systems
Delayed/yellow until rechecked by a paramedic
Immediate/red after five rescue breaths fail

explanation: START and similar systems tag non-breathing after airway maneuver as expectant when resources constrained. This applies when there are no spontaneous respirations after the airway is opened and resources are limited.

distractorExplanations.a: Red applies when breathing resumes after airway positioning; apnea that persists after repositioning is expectant/black.
distractorExplanations.c: Delayed is for patients who breathe but cannot walk and lack immediate threats; apneic patients are not held as yellow.
distractorExplanations.d: In JumpSTART, a child still apneic after 5 rescue breaths is tagged expectant, not immediate.

prompt: Consent for treatment of an unconscious adult is generally

options.text: Expressed consent from the nearest bystander
Informed consent obtained once the patient wakes
Implied consent for emergency care
Involuntary consent ordered by medical direction

explanation: Implied consent allows emergency treatment when patient cannot consent and delay would harm.

distractorExplanations.a: Bystanders have no legal authority to consent for an adult; unconscious adults are treated under implied consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for the patient to wake could cause harm; emergency care proceeds under implied consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Involuntary consent applies to patients in custody or under court order, not to unconscious adults needing care.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: An EMR discovers possible child abuse during a call. Appropriate action includes:

options.text: Report only if the child confirms the abuse to you
Confront the caregiver at the scene and ask them to explain the injuries
Document suspicion of abuse as a diagnosis on the PCR
Report per local mandatory reporting laws and ensure child safety

explanation: Mandatory reporters must notify appropriate authorities and document objective findings.

distractorExplanations.a: Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion; a disclosure or confession is not required.
distractorExplanations.b: Confrontation can escalate danger to the child and crew; document objectively and report to authorities instead.
distractorExplanations.c: The PCR records objective findings and quotes; EMRs do not record abuse as a diagnosis.

prompt: Vehicle staging at a violent scene should be

options.text: At a safe distance until law enforcement secures scene
In front of the residence to speed patient access
Close by with lights on so police can locate the unit
Directly behind the first police car as it arrives

explanation: Staging protects crews until scene is safe or escorted by law enforcement. Stage upwind/uphill when hazards are also present.

distractorExplanations.b: Parking at the door exposes the crew; stage out of sight until law enforcement clears the scene.
distractorExplanations.c: Lights and nearby staging draw attention at a violent scene; stage out of sight with lights off.
distractorExplanations.d: Entering with police before the scene is secured places the crew in danger; wait until it is declared safe.

prompt: After patient transfer to ALS, the EMR should

options.text: Hand over the patient and send the PCR next week
Provide concise verbal report and complete PCR
Give a full head-to-toe report while ALS treats
Leave once ALS has the patient; ALS documents care

explanation: Handoff communication and complete documentation ensure continuity of care. Include times and interventions in the PCR.

distractorExplanations.a: The PCR is completed promptly so receiving providers have the record; a delayed report breaks continuity of care.
distractorExplanations.c: Handoff reports are concise and prioritized; long reports during treatment distract the receiving crew.
distractorExplanations.d: Each provider documents their own care; the EMR must still complete a PCR for the care given.

prompt: Which action violates ethical boundaries?

options.text: Reporting a coworker who appears impaired on duty
Respecting cultural preferences when safe
Accepting a large cash gift from a patient
Thanking a family for a homemade card after a call

explanation: Accepting gifts for preferential treatment creates conflict of interest and unethical conduct. A gift tied to preferential future response is a clear conflict of interest.

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting impairment is an ethical duty that protects patients; it does not violate professional boundaries.
distractorExplanations.b: Cultural respect within safety limits is appropriate.
distractorExplanations.d: Accepting a small token of thanks with no expectation of favors is generally acceptable; the problem is a gift for preference.

prompt: When terminating resuscitation in the field is considered (per protocol/medical direction), factors include?

options.text: Patient age over 80 with a long history of heart disease
No shock advised on the first AED analysis
Family request to stop even without a valid DNR
Downtime without ROSC and medical direction criteria

explanation: Termination follows protocol/medical direction considering downtime, DNR, scene safety, and futility criteria. A valid DNR and an unsafe scene are also considered.

distractorExplanations.a: Age and comorbidity alone are not termination criteria; protocols use downtime, ROSC, DNR, and medical direction.
distractorExplanations.b: A no-shock message does not mean futility; CPR continues per protocol until termination criteria are met.
distractorExplanations.c: Verbal family wishes without a valid DNR do not meet termination criteria; medical direction decides.
